name: 贅食家千壽 丸の内店 (Zeishokuya Senju Marunouchi)

claims.text: No information on dedicated fryers or separation of wheat-containing preparations. The parent menu includes tempura, indicating wheat flour is used in the kitchen.
Standard Japanese soy sauce (wheat-containing) is the default at sushi restaurants. No gluten-free soy sauce or tamari was mentioned anywhere in available sources.
Seafood-based dashi (海鮮出汁) is used in miso soup. Fish and shellfish are prepared throughout the kitchen. No plant-based separation is available.
No allergy menu, allergen labeling, or staff allergy-handling protocol was found in any source. Celiac diners should call ahead: 052-201-3655.
Counter-style seating means you can communicate directly with the chef about what goes into each piece, which may allow some customization.

name: アフタヌーンティー ロシェ (Afternoon Tea Rocher)

claims.text: The entire menu is built on wheat (scones, pastries, cakes, quiche, pies, biscuits), so cross-contamination is inherent and the venue is not suitable for celiacs. No gluten-free handling is documented.
Dishes are prepared with shared dairy, eggs and meat (prosciutto, anchovy); no vegan preparation or separation is documented.

Menu items and ingredients (Nara-vegetable quiche, carrot salad, prosciutto cake salé, anchovy fish pie, local-tea scones, named petit fours) are described in detail by published articles, helping diners identify what they are eating, though no formal allergen program is documented.
As a standard izakaya cooking on shared equipment with wheat-based seasonings, cross-contamination with gluten should be assumed throughout.
Home-style izakaya dishes here rely on standard Japanese seasonings such as soy sauce, which is brewed with wheat.
The menu is built around meat and fish (e.g. grilled chicken-thigh steak) and dashi, so vegan cross-contact is expected.
The café bakes its own wheat shokupan in-house and serves it as toast, so flour and gluten are present on-site; no gluten-free preparation is documented.
Milk is used for the WHITE espresso drink and butter/honey for the toast; no documented separation for vegan orders.
The owner is a licensed English-speaking guide, so dietary questions can be asked directly in English.

name: アンヌ・マリーカフェ (Anne-Marie Cafe)

claims.text: The menu is built around wheat flour (scones, cakes, quiche, sandwiches), so cross-contact with gluten is unavoidable throughout the kitchen.
Baked goods and the afternoon tea set use dairy (clotted cream, butter) and eggs; no plant-based preparation is documented.
The cafe states that allergy accommodations are possible (アレルギー対応も可); diners with allergies should ask directly.
Allergy accommodations are noted as available, so guests can discuss needs with staff before ordering.
Menu is built on toast, sandwiches, hot dogs, pasta, and curry — wheat is pervasive throughout the kitchen, so cross-contact is effectively unavoidable.
Core offerings rely on eggs, dairy (yogurt), and meat; no plant-based menu is documented.
Core dishes rely on flour-based demi-glace sauce and breaded cutlets, so wheat is pervasive across the kitchen; no gluten-free preparation is documented.
The menu is meat- and dairy-centric (hamburg steak, demi-glace, consommé, beef cutlet); no vegan options or separate preparation are documented.
Wheat gluten (seitan) is a core menu ingredient prepared in the same kitchen, so cross-contact with gluten is unavoidable; the venue is not suitable for celiacs.
Yogurt (dairy) is used in the spicy curry sauce and eggs are used in omurice/omelette dishes, so vegans must request egg-, milk-, and yogurt-free preparations.
Staff are described as friendly and happy to explain the food, and dishes made without egg, milk, or yogurt are available on request.
Fully meat- and fish-free kitchen using organic, pesticide-free vegetables and brown rice, with many naturally vegan curry options.
English-language menu and barrier-free accommodations (braille menu, guide dogs welcome) make ordering and asking about ingredients easier for foreign visitors.
